title: Rental statement capture
description: Attach the managing agent's rental statement to a rent payment and record the agency fees it charges, replacing an estimate derived from management_fee_pct with the actual figures and shipping the statement as tax-pack evidence.

context.reference_document: Statement #1 - OWN10905, Rich & Oliva, 28 Nov 2025, 56 Forbes St Croydon Park NSW 2133
context.defect_corrected: Agent fees computed as weeks x weekly_rent x management_fee_pct at tax-pack/page.tsx:281-286 can only reproduce recurring percentage charges. On the reference statement it captures the $242 management fee and misses $1,251.80 of letting fee, lease fee and bank charges, and is presented with no estimate disclosure.
context.approach: Extend rental_payments in place rather than introduce a statement table, because rows already exist in production. Additive nullable columns only.
context.amended_during_implementation: Phase 1.5 and FR12/FR13 were added after verifying FR1. lib/email-parser/parse-statement.ts:51 instructs the model to store the NET disbursed amount in rental_payments.amount, which lib/tax/rental-income.ts reports as gross rent — understating assessable income on every email-ingested payment. Found in code, not in data entry, so the original out-of-scope 'known risk' framing was wrong. Also recorded: statement fees are GST-inclusive while the management_fee_pct estimate is not.

decisions.decision: Extend rental_payments rather than add a rental_statements table
decisions.why: Rows already exist in production and one statement maps to one payment row in current practice. Avoids a data migration entirely.

decisions.decision: Itemised fee columns rather than a single agent-fees total
decisions.why: Management fee is a percentage and letting/lease fees are one-off. Itemising is what lets the recorded management fee be cross-checked against the percentage estimate specifically, rather than against a lumped total.

decisions.decision: sundry_fees feeds the ATO sundry line, not the commission line
decisions.why: Bank and administrative charges are what the sundry line is for, and keeping them out of the commission line keeps the agent-fees figure directly comparable to the estimate it replaces.

decisions.decision: other_outgoings is recorded for reconciliation and never deducted
decisions.why: Third-party costs the agent paid arrive via their own invoice, which is the only path that classifies them correctly as Division 40 rather than an immediate deduction. Deducting them from the statement as well would double-count.

decisions.decision: Confirmed statement fees are the actual; the percentage estimate is a labelled fallback, never summed
decisions.why: The statement's $242 is exactly what the 5.5% calculation produces, so summing double-counts it. The fallback means nothing regresses for properties with no statement uploaded.

decisions.decision: lib/xero/mapper.ts:246 left on the percentage estimate
decisions.why: It posts real journals. Changing what it writes needs its own track and verification against a real tenant.

open_risks: CONFIRMED AND NOW IN SCOPE (Phase 1.5): rental_payments.amount holds net received for every email-ingested row because parse-statement.ts:51 instructs it, while actualRentForFy reports it as gross rent. 6 of 7 local rows affected. Understates assessable income.
Correcting rows 2-7 requires the original statements; a row without its source document stays flagged rather than back-solved from an assumed fee percentage.
Once the parser is repointed, live ingestion writes different values into `amount`. Rows ingested between the parser fix and the historical correction must not be double-corrected.
Double-counting third-party costs is the primary failure mode; guarded by FR8 and acceptance criterion 5 but must be checked in review.
Financial position view and the tax pack must agree on the agent-fee figure; they are wired to a shared resolver but there is no automated coverage for either surface.
AI extraction of rental statements has not been run against any agent's format other than Rich & Oliva.
